positive: Mid-word subword continuation tokens inside compound/derived English words, especially 'emb[oss]ing'/'emb[ossed]' (embossing), and similar word-internal pieces like 'Story[t]ellers' or the particle 'out' in phrasal verbs ('branch out'). Wikipedia text about crafts/printing/arts.
negative: Commas following a noun phrase or clause in Wikipedia prose (' ,' after a title, place name, or time adverb like 'later'), plus some word-internal subword tokens like 'dis[m]asted'.

positive: Word-internal or rare-name subword tokens in Wikipedia text, especially non-English/indigenous names (Māori 'P[ā]kehā'), place names ('Esc[an]aba'), and some technical nouns/verb pieces ('memory', 'ref-itted'). Fires on the 2nd piece of a rare proper noun or word.
negative: First subword token of rare proper/technical names, especially biological taxonomy and mycology ('My-cenaceae', 'my-c-ologist', 'moll-uscs') and European surnames/place names ('Mess-ines', 'G-orm-ley'). Natural-history/scientific nomenclature.

positive: Math word-problem reasoning in structured bullet outlines: the bullet marker '*' starting a new item right after a '**Goal:**' line (leading into '**Format**'), and tokens referring back to the problem text ('In it', 'already planted') when restating the problem.
negative: Content nouns/values inside bulleted problem analysis: object names ('gift'), digits in money amounts, person names after 'Person 3:', and key words in quoted constraints ('Missing Week', 'Missed one'). Weak magnitudes.

positive: Biology/species descriptions: tokens right after a species name subject that introduce its definition or description ('X , known as ..., [is] a species', 'is [a]', '[It] may grow'), and words like 'introduced' (species), 'plant' in organism names. Encyclopedic animal/plant articles, very strong activations.
negative: Function words in mid-sentence of zoological detail (reproduction: 'carried by females [for]', 'carrying eggs [are]') and word-internal subword pieces of taxonomic/biological Latin names ('Cycli-oph-ora', 'mycor-rh-izal', 'leafc-utter').

positive: Second part of East Asian (Chinese) personal names ('Wai [Lin]', 'Du Z[ong]wu'), possessive 's after names, and 'of' in institutional names 'Protection [of] ...'. Weak.
negative: Word-internal pieces of German/European surnames ('Gott[sch]alk', 'Lance [Henri]ksen', 'Chris [S]abin') — the middle of a multi-token Germanic/Scandinavian name — and LaTeX environment names ('\end{[pm]atrix}').

positive: Tokens immediately after a closing quotation mark in Wikipedia prose (attribution 'said', parenthetical '(' citing the speaker), citation boilerplate like '. Retrieved', and items in lists of titles (Shakespeare plays). Weak.
negative: The token 'step' in the fixed math prompt suffix 'Please reason step by step,' following a word-problem question. Very consistent.

positive: Latinate or foreign word-final suffix pieces: Latin species epithets ending '-ii' ('hall[ii]', 'ross[ii]'), '-ium' ('bienn[ium]'), '-alia' ('Westph[alia]'), and romanized Chinese syllables ('Guoz[ij]ian'). Botany/geography in Wikipedia.
negative: Pieces inside German compound words ('Relig[ions]-'), CJK characters in Chinese book titles ('書'), and acronym pieces ('R[IA]A').

positive: Math reasoning nested bullet lists of computed values: tokens after a calculation line such as newline/indentation whitespace, 'so far' in running totals, 'Start' labels, line breaks after 'Quantity: 20'. Inside step-by-step arithmetic tallies.
negative: Header/label words in bold or section titles: '**[Goal]**:' in math analysis outlines and Wikipedia section headings '= = [Battle] = ='. The first word of a heading/label.

positive: Fraction/quantity words like 'one' in 'one-fourth' following a comma or 'is' in math problems; also adjective/derivative suffixes ('-ish', '-uration') and nationality adjectives in lists ('combined Canadian, British'). Mixed.
negative: Self-correction / meta-reasoning markers in model math reasoning: '*[Self]-Correction', 'let me [re]-calculate', 'let me [re]-read', 'step[-by]-step'. The hyphenated prefix piece of reasoning-process words. Very strong.

positive: Plural/count nouns that are the counted object in a quantity phrase ('specific [items]', 'pieces of [pizza]', 'fifteen [players]') and abstract nouns after 'and' ('intelligence').
negative: The preposition 'of' after a quantifying/abstract noun head: 'the kind [of]', 'hints [of]', 'sense [of]', 'portion [of]'. Strongest on 'kind of'.
